reasoning: Both are mostly accurate, but B is far closer to what this designer asked for. B keeps an observation log with IDs and separates seen [O] from inferred [I] and hypothesis [H], and its pixel claims check out against the screenshots. Each cross-site pattern says when it transfers and why, and the 'avoid mixing' advice is reasoned. Its self-review names weak evidence, such as the A/B test cohorts and the indirect motion evidence. A is concise and readable but mostly describes the pages. Its claims can't be traced to specific evidence, and it slips into UI critique and 1–5 'reference value' scores. B is long and full of IDs, but the comparison file still reads well on its own.
a_strengths: Short, scannable comparison table and one-line contrast that a designer grasps fast
Correctly notes the shared page skeleton (hero, logo wall, bento, stats, testimonials, closing CTA) and the different 'skins'
Marks estimated type values as '推測'; concrete colors match the screenshots
Practical 'reuse as-is / pick by positioning / avoid' conclusion
a_weaknesses: No evidence IDs, so claims can't be traced to a specific screenshot region or source line
Mostly description; little reasoning about why each choice works for each audience
Doesn't flag A/B test cohorts or that motion evidence is indirect
Patterns have no conditions for when they transfer
b_strengths: Full evidence chain (S-/P-/M-/H-/I-/X- IDs) with E1-E5 evidence grades; claims are traceable
[O]/[I]/[H] labels used consistently, and each [H] comes with a way to verify it
Spots conflicts in the data (branding textPrimary vs sampled pixels, Stripe test cohorts differing by width, blank mobile region)

Design-language table explains the trade-offs (payments product vs collaboration tool, portal vs single funnel); 'avoid mixing' advice is reasoned
b_weaknesses: Very long, with heavy ID/label jargon (VP/XP/DP/E-levels) that slows reading
Observations cite tablet screenshots that are missing from the folder
